text: Everything so far in this course has taught you how individual platforms work and how to read their real specifications honestly. This lesson is where that knowledge turns into a decision: given an actual workload, which platform would you actually pick, and why?

The wrong way to choose hardware is to start with which vendor has the biggest number and work backward. The right way is to characterize the workload first: how many qubits does it need, how deep is the circuit, what does its connectivity pattern actually look like, and how error-tolerant is the result allowed to be. Only once those four answers exist does it make sense to go look at platforms — at that point you're matching requirements to tradeoffs instead of being talked into a number.

Four realistic shapes keep showing up. Shallow, many-qubit, noise-tolerant workloads — like variational algorithms — favor whichever platform offers the most usable qubits at acceptable fidelity, historically superconducting. Deep, few-qubit, high-fidelity-required workloads reward the best gate fidelity and coherence per qubit, historically trapped-ion. Workloads needing all-to-all connectivity favor trapped-ion or photonic's native long-range reach over a sparse grid. And naturally local, nearest-neighbor workloads play to superconducting's fabrication strengths, or to neutral-atom arrays whose reconfigurable tweezers can be arranged to match the topology before the circuit even runs.

A technically ideal platform you can't actually use yet isn't a useful recommendation. Cloud access and cost: is it available where you already have billing set up, and what does a real run actually cost at your shot count? Queue time: a technically superior platform with a multi-day queue may be wrong for an iterative workflow. SDK and toolchain maturity: an elegant piece of hardware with an immature SDK can cost more engineering time than it saves in fidelity. And vendor roadmap: will this platform still be supported and improving a year from now?

A real recommendation names the workload's requirements, names the platform, and names what was given up to get there — because every real choice trades something away. Next lesson, the course's capstone, asks you to write exactly this kind of decision down formally, as a brief a real stakeholder could act on.
